name: Neoconservatism
summary: Neoconservatism grew from American anti-Stalinist liberals who turned against the New Left and the Great Society and came to favor free-market growth, cultural traditionalism and an assertive foreign policy. It supports American military primacy, confrontation with hostile regimes, and promotion of democracy, with limited trust in international institutions. Domestically it accepts a reduced but real welfare state and treats culture and morality as political matters.
scope: The mainstream American movement from Irving Kristol, Norman Podhoretz and Jeane Kirkpatrick in the 1970s-80s to the Kristol-Kagan PNAC network and the Bush-era foreign policy. It does not cover the pre-1970s liberal-hawk precursors or non-American uses of the term.

keyFigures.name: Irving Kristol
keyFigures.role: Called the godfather of neoconservatism; coined and popularized the label.

keyFigures.name: Norman Podhoretz
keyFigures.role: Editor of Commentary, which became a key neoconservative publication.

keyFigures.name: Jeane Kirkpatrick
keyFigures.role: Author of Dictatorships and Double Standards and Reagan's UN ambassador.

sources.usedFor: Kristol's two cheers for capitalism, supply-side, welfare views, imperial role remark.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Neoconservatives accept a limited welfare state on practical grounds and were never defined by health policy, so adherents split.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Not a defining issue; neoconservatives favor growth-first economics but did not campaign against wage floors as a matter of principle.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: They give a qualified endorsement of free markets, while holding that markets lack moral guidance.

public-ownership.rationale: Kristol and the Public Interest circle stressed the unintended harms of government planning and favored private enterprise.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Kristol describes neoconservatives as favoring lower tax rates to encourage growth.

cut-welfare.rationale: They favor a reduced welfare state limited by practical rather than principled concerns, rejecting most Great Society programs but keeping the New Deal core.

strong-leader.rationale: They favor a strong presidency in foreign affairs but have no doctrine of bypassing gridlock; adherents split.

state-harmful.rationale: Kristol rejects the limited-government case as a historical eccentricity and says people prefer strong government to weak government.

empower-police-military.rationale: Calls for large defense spending increases and a dominant military are central, and they stress law and order against the counterculture.

traditional-family.rationale: They allied with religious traditionalists and treat social questions as moral ones.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Older neoconservatives opposed it, though younger ones diverge.

more-religion-public.rationale: Kristol describes an alliance with religious traditionalists on schooling, church-state relations and pornography, and he sees religion as moral ballast for capitalism.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: They supported civil rights and integration but opposed racial preferences and the Black Power turn.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Kristol calls patriotism a natural and healthy sentiment that institutions should foster, and laments cultural decline.

gradual-change.rationale: They stress unintended consequences of social engineering, and Kirkpatrick argues democracy takes decades to build.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Kristol ties American identity to being a nation of immigrants; no restrictionist platform, though not a core issue.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Kristol writes that world government is a terrible idea that can lead to world tyranny and that institutions pointing toward it deserve the deepest suspicion; PNAC rejected tying US action to UN Security Council approval.

nation-first.rationale: They favor US action without Security Council consent and prize US interest and leadership, while framing it as serving wider freedom.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Kristol says the US will always feel obliged to defend a democratic nation under attack, and neoconservatives backed democratic and humanitarian causes by force.

limit-growth.rationale: Economic growth is the steady focus of Kristol's neoconservatism.

revolution-justified.rationale: Kirkpatrick argues revolutionary regimes tend to be worse than traditional autocracies, and neoconservatives oppose radical social upheaval.

experts-over-public.rationale: They built policy journals such as The Public Interest but also attacked the left's new class of intellectuals.

central-planning.rationale: The Public Interest circle documented the unintended harms of planning and Kristol rejects socialism.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: They are former socialists who embraced capitalism, giving it two cheers.

one-party-rule.rationale: They defend democracy and democratic allies, and Kirkpatrick opposes totalitarian regimes.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Kirkpatrick defends traditional autocrats as allies, but this is not a view about monarchy as such.

democracy-best.rationale: They promote democracy abroad on the basis of universal natural rights, but Kirkpatrick warns it is tenable only with culture and institutions, and Kristol laments democratic vulgarity.

natural-rulers.rationale: Straussian influence points toward elites, but neoconservatives also embrace democracy.

war-builds-character.rationale: Their emphasis is on moral clarity and strength, not war as a character-builder.

separate-church-state.rationale: Kristol discusses an alliance with religious traditionalists on church-state relations.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: They value religion's moral role but not theocratic law.

military-superiority.rationale: PNAC and Kristol call for preserving US military preeminence and large defense spending.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Kristol grounds American patriotism in an ideological nation of immigrants.

equal-outcomes.rationale: They rejected Great Society equalization and socialism, and favor growth over redistribution.

self-interest-moral.rationale: They hold that markets lack moral guidance, and Kristol speaks of capitalism's spiritual malaise.

duties-before-rights.rationale: They stress civic virtue and patriotism but also natural rights.

accelerate-technology.rationale: They value gradual change and institutions over disruption.

restore-past-order.rationale: Kristol's neoconservatism is a governing persuasion that accepts modern democracy rather than seeking a lost order.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Kristol calls neoconservatism a persuasion rather than an ideology and stresses the unintended consequences of doctrinaire policy.

distribute-by-need.rationale: They are ex-socialists who reject this principle.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: They are anti-Stalinist, anti-Communist and defend democracy.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: They reject Marxist theory and see US power as a force for freedom.

taxation-theft.rationale: Kristol rejects limited-government libertarianism as a historical eccentricity.

harm-principle.rationale: They want government to attend to moral and cultural questions beyond harm.

media-academia-power.rationale: Neoconservatives attacked the adversary culture of the new class in media and universities, though the claim about power over elected officials is a stretch.

total-state.rationale: Anti-totalitarian; Kirkpatrick draws sharp lines against totalitarian regimes.

territorial-expansion.rationale: They want expanded US influence and leadership but not territorial conquest; Kristol speaks of an imperial role.

bound-labor.rationale: Serfdom is never discussed by neoconservative writers; rejection is assumed from their defence of free markets and liberal democracy.

universal-morality.rationale: They ground democracy promotion in universal natural rights and moral clarity.

single-common-good.rationale: Straussian strands incline that way, but the movement accepts democratic pluralism.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: They are strong supporters of Israel.

school-vouchers.rationale: Kristol cites education quality as a neoconservative concern, and many back choice.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Kristol says neoconservatives prefer to avoid big deficits but will accept them as the temporary cost of growth, being more relaxed than classical liberals.

force-without-un.rationale: PNAC's Iraq letter said US policy must not be crippled by insistence on Security Council unanimity, and the 2002 strategy accepted preemption.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Kristol sees religion and tradition as necessary moral ballast that reason alone cannot supply, so faith and custom are valid guides alongside reason.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Kristol criticized welfare dependency and neoconservatives backed work requirements, accepting aid only as a reduced safety net.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Kristol stresses cultural traditionalism, religion and the moral weight of inherited institutions.

dominated-front.rationale: Neoconservatives champion American primacy and confrontation with hostile regimes rather than a bloc against the West.

ban-interest.rationale: Kristol gives two cheers for capitalism and favors market-led growth, which rests on lending at interest.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Neoconservatism grew from liberals who supported civil rights and universal natural rights, and the movement opposes racial classification in law.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Neoconservatism arose in opposition to Marxism and the New Left, and treats the state as an instrument of national purpose.

elite-replacement.rationale: Neoconservatives are establishment-minded and pro-immigrant in the American tradition; a deliberate elite replacement plot is a conspiracy theory outside their worldview.

national-mission.rationale: Neoconservatives hold that America has a mission to promote democracy abroad, and PNAC calls for a foreign policy that promotes American principles globally.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Neoconservatives criticize the "new class" of liberal elites as out of touch, but they themselves belong to the political establishment and do not call it corrupt.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Kristol rejects a purely minimal state, accepting a reduced welfare state and treating culture and morality as political matters, and neoconservatives favor a strong military and active foreign policy.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Kirkpatrick treats legitimacy as resting on elections and popular participation, and neoconservatives promote democracy abroad, though they stress order and culture too.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Preemption, regime change and military primacy mean they accept initiating force for security and democratic goals.

vanguard-party.rationale: Neoconservatism began as a break by ex-Marxists and anti-Stalinists from Leninist politics and opposes revolutionary vanguards.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Post-9/11 neoconservatives backed strong security powers, yet they claim to defend constitutional democracy, so adherents split.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Kristol's neoconservatism accepts markets as the engine of growth and opposes price controls except as a rare emergency measure.

party-controls-media.rationale: Neoconservatives champion democracy promotion and free expression against totalitarian regimes, so state control of media contradicts their core view.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Neoconservatives stress assimilation and patriotism but the sources set no residency period, so adherents split.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Kristol rejects world government and neoconservatives distrust binding international bodies in favor of national sovereignty and American leadership.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is not a neoconservative concern and the movement is religiously mixed (Jewish, Catholic, Protestant), so adherents have no common view.

clerical-rule.rationale: No neoconservative source discusses rule by clergy; although they value religion in public life, rejection is assumed from their liberal-democratic commitments.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Kristol stresses patriotism as a healthy sentiment and the movement champions national defense and American power, the opposite of revolutionary defeatism.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: PNAC's statement of principles calls for American primacy, a larger military and strengthened ties with allies, so ending alliances and withdrawing troops contradicts it.

people-in-arms.rationale: PNAC calls for more defense spending and a stronger professional military to preserve US primacy, the opposite of replacing it with an armed citizenry.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Neoconservatives promote democracy abroad and held that growth is not a reason to accept authoritarianism, though Kirkpatrick tolerated friendly autocracies for strategic reasons.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Neoconservatives were strongly pro-Israel and many opposed territorial concessions, but others backed negotiated settlements, so adherents are split on this principle.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Kristol held that capitalism needs moral and religious grounding, but neoconservatives did not accept community limits on property as a principle; adherents split.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Neoconservatives, as anti-Stalinist ex-leftists, treated the Soviet Union as a totalitarian communist state and did not accept the Trotskyist state-capitalist label.

collective-defense.rationale: Neoconservatives champion NATO and US alliances as the base of American primacy, and PNAC calls for strengthening ties with allies.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Kristol's persuasion values religion as a pillar of moral order and opposes state hostility to religious institutions.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Supply-siders in the movement favor lower marginal rates, but Kristol accepted progressive taxation; adherents are split.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The movement presents itself as defending constitutional democracy and rule of law against totalitarianism.

leader-cult.rationale: Neoconservatives condemned totalitarian leader worship, and Kirkpatrick's distinction rests on it.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Neoconservatives broke from Marxism and reject class struggle as a frame.

land-redistribution.rationale: They defend private property and growth-oriented capitalism, so forced redistribution of estates is rejected.

refugee-return.rationale: Not a defining issue; adherents are split.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Kristol and others stress culture, ideas and morality as political drivers after leaving Marxism.

ban-cartels.rationale: Not a defining issue; growth-first economics without a stated antitrust line.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Kristol supports open global capitalism and growth; autarky is far from the neoconservative position.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Kristol calls patriotism a natural and healthy sentiment that institutions should foster, which favours nation-centred history.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Kristol remarks on America's quasi-imperial role but neoconservatives frame intervention as democracy promotion, so adherents are split.

patriotic-education.rationale: Kristol says patriotism should be fostered by institutions and laments cultural decline.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Former socialists who gave capitalism two cheers, they hold that it is resilient and growth-producing.

delink-world-market.rationale: Kristol stresses growth through market economics; poor countries are expected to integrate.

elective-rulers.rationale: Democracy promotion rests on the view that legitimate government comes from elections, which Kirkpatrick treats as the test of democracy.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Kristol's account stresses patriotism, civic engagement and treating politics and culture as serious matters, the opposite of withdrawal.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: The claim is a Marxist-Gramscian one that neoconservatives reject, though Kristol's theory of a liberal 'new class' shaping culture is a partial parallel.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Kristol's pro-growth capitalism holds that markets and trade raise living standards, rejecting dependency and exploitation theories.

native-born-offices.rationale: Neoconservatives were largely descendants of immigrants and defend a creedal American nationhood, so reserving offices by birth conflicts with it.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Kirkpatrick and the movement condemn totalitarian systems of left and right, communism above all, though she separated them from traditional autocracies.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: The movement did not address it, and adherents are split.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Neoconservatism holds liberal-democratic institutions to be universally applicable and worth promoting, though Kirkpatrick warned that democracy cannot be installed quickly anywhere.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Neoconservatives support civilian control of the military and an elected executive; a political guardian role for the armed forces is outside their program.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Neoconservatism arose partly from opposition to Great Society racial quotas and affirmative action, and treats discrimination as unequal treatment.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Kristol defended capitalism and bourgeois society while criticising its culture; adherents split.

democratic-peace.rationale: Spreading democracy to make the world safer is a core neoconservative claim in the PNAC network and Bush-era policy.

non-intervention.rationale: They hold that regimes can and should be confronted for external or domestic reasons, rejecting strict non-intervention.

industrial-unions.rationale: Market-oriented and sceptical of unions; no stated view on form.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Limited trust in international institutions and a preference for American primacy and unilateral action are documented.

religious-nation.rationale: Defends cultural traditionalism and the moral role of religion, but defines the nation politically (American creed), not religiously.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Neoconservatives want America itself to be the leading power and reject deference to other states, as the PNAC statement of principles stresses American primacy.

defeat-communism.rationale: Neoconservatism arose from anti-Stalinism, and Kirkpatrick's argument was that Soviet totalitarianism had to be confronted, not accommodated.

religion-illusion.rationale: Kristol argued that religion is essential to a healthy society and that the Enlightenment-style hope of its fading is mistaken.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Kristol gave two cheers for capitalism for its growth and wealth creation and neoconservatives favour market growth as the base of a good society.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Neoconservatives favour market capitalism, the nation-state and a strong national identity, which stand against common-property communities.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Neoconservatives treat capitalism as the sound basis of a free society and communism as the enemy, so there is no third way to seek.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Neoconservatives are often strong supporters of Israel, but the sources document no principle that historical ties outweigh present claims.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Kristol-style cultural traditionalism does not extend, in the sources, to criminal penalties for private conduct.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Neoconservatives promote democratization abroad and defend liberal-democratic order at home, though Kirkpatrick tolerated allied autocracies.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Representative democracy is preferred over direct participation; neoconservatives opposed the New Left's participatory politics.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Neoconservatism arose in reaction to the New Left and identity-based politics.

alienated-labor.rationale: Kristol offers two cheers for capitalism and rejects the left's critique of it.

social-market-economy.rationale: Kristol accepts a reduced but real welfare state alongside growth-oriented markets and supply-side policy.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The PNAC statement calls for higher defence spending and American military primacy.

rich-first.rationale: Neoconservatives put growth ahead of equality and accept inequality as the price of it.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: The PNAC statement of principles calls for the United States to strengthen ties with its democratic allies and challenge hostile regimes, and neoconservatives backed NATO and its expansion.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Neoconservatives emphasise traditional culture and morality, but the movement was never defined by this issue and its adherents are split.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Neoconservatism treats religion and traditional morality as important to a healthy society, so state promotion of unbelief is the opposite of its view.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Kristol and the movement criticised the Great Society and expansive state programs and praised civil-society institutions, accepting only a reduced welfare state.

term-limits.rationale: Neoconservatives have no doctrine on term limits; some conservatives backed them, but neoconservatives value experienced statesmen; adherents split.

vote-delegation.rationale: Liquid democracy is never discussed; rejection is assumed from the movement's preference for representative institutions over direct popular rule.

rent-control.rationale: Neoconservatives broke with the Great Society and endorse market growth; price controls are inconsistent with Kristol's account.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: The PNAC statement and neoconservative foreign policy call for forward American military presence overseas, which presupposes foreign bases and, for allies, welcoming them.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: A movement committed to military primacy and confronting hostile regimes rejects absolute pacifism and holds that force is sometimes required.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Neoconservatives frame world politics in moral terms of good and evil, as in the confrontation with the Soviet Union and tyranny, though not in strictly spiritual language.

municipal-property.rationale: Kristol defended capitalism and private enterprise, rejecting collective ownership.

family-wage.rationale: Kristol accepted a safety net but favoured supply-side growth; no stated wage doctrine.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Kristol argued religion is needed for social order and culture, favouring a politics that serves more than material ends.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Neoconservatism is universalist, built on liberal democratic principles, not on racial group interests.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: PNAC and neoconservatives urge preemption and military force to promote democracy, not defence alone.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Neoconservatives define the nation by civic, democratic creed and not by language or ethnicity.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: The movement is outward-facing and sees America as a dominant power, not as a target of partition plots.

arms-reduction.rationale: PNAC and Kirkpatrick-style neoconservatism call for rebuilding and expanding American military power and primacy.

capital-controls.rationale: Neoconservatism embraces free-market growth and open capital flows as part of its economic outlook.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Kristol's patriotism and the PNAC stress on military strength and readiness make refusal to fight an anathema.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: They defend US primacy and the existing liberal order and distrust international institutions that would redistribute power or wealth.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Neoconservatives are institutionalists who want to use and strengthen the American state, not destroy it.

sacred-nation.rationale: Kristol treats patriotism as natural and healthy and sees the nation as a moral community, although he does not call it sacred.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Neoconservatives call for American military primacy and large defence spending, and treat unilateral disarmament as unacceptable; PNAC's statement of principles stresses strength.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Kristol valued religion's role in public morality yet American neoconservatives accept constitutional religious pluralism; no stated position on legal precedence.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Neoconservatives promote democracy abroad but Kirkpatrick and Kristol also stress culture, institutions and values beyond elections; adherents split.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Kristol accepted a limited welfare state on practical grounds, and some neoconservatives liked Friedman-style schemes while others kept existing programs; split.

women-suffrage.rationale: No cited source discusses women's political rights; agreement is assumed from the movement's commitment to American liberal democracy.

race-social-construct.rationale: Neoconservatives opposed racial preferences and favoured colour-blind policy, but the sources open no statement on the scientific status of race; split.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Neoconservatives accept property rights and markets on practical grounds but never took a first-claim theory of ownership as a position.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Neoconservatism came from anti-Stalinism, and Kirkpatrick's Dictatorships and Double Standards treats communist states as the enemy to be opposed.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: No documented position in the sources opened; adherents are split between self-determination and unitary-state views.

close-ties-china.rationale: PNAC and neoconservative writers treat a rising China as a strategic competitor to be balanced, not a partner to lean on in place of the US.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Neoconservatives accepted a reduced welfare state and criticized the universal Great Society programs, favoring help aimed at real need.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Kristol accepts market outcomes and doubts equalising redistribution, though he also accepts a limited welfare state.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: Neoconservatives favour free-market growth and are wary of new taxes and global regulation; not a documented issue.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Neoconservatives attacked racial preferences and Great Society programs as counterproductive; stated in the sources only in general terms.

multipolar-world.rationale: PNAC and Kristol-Kagan call for US primacy and distrust international institutions as constraints on it.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Neoconservatism grew from anti-Stalinism and opposes communist rule.

police-more-powers.rationale: Calls for large defense spending increases and a dominant military are central, and they stress law and order against the counterculture. (Moved from empower-police-military, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about military spending alone.)

missingStatements.text: My country should be willing to use force without approval from the UN Security Council.
missingStatements.rationale: PNAC's Iraq letter said US policy must not be crippled by insistence on Security Council unanimity, and the 2002 strategy accepted preemption.

missingStatements.text: Spreading democracy abroad should be a goal of my country's foreign policy.
missingStatements.rationale: Neoconservatives ground democracy promotion in universal natural rights and PNAC calls for promoting political and economic freedom abroad.

notes: Many economic and social answers are low confidence because neoconservatism is defined mainly by foreign policy and its break with the left. Paleo-conservative critics and later strands differ on immigration, trade and same-sex marriage.
